name: Admiral
workload: Complex and real 1-D (19 lengths for the FFTW comparison, 61 for ducc0) and N-D (9 shapes for FFTW, 27 for ducc0) FFTs in float and double on a 16-core AVX-512 Xeon, timed with nanobench (min across repetitions) after an accuracy gate against a reference DFT.
claimed_speedup: At 1 thread beats FFTW_MEASURE by 1.34x (1-D) and 1.43x (N-D), both precisions pooled; vs ducc0 at 1 thread 2.18x (f64) / 2.70x (f32) on 1-D, 1.12x / 1.41x on 2-D, 1.60x / 1.67x on 3-D; at 16 threads vs ducc0 2-D 1.27x / 1.58x and 3-D 2.67x / 3.53x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, -march=native (CMake release preset; further flags not listed; sweep of 2026-08-24 per benchmark/README.md)
hardware: Intel Xeon w5-3435X (16 physical cores, AVX-512)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (earliest commit visible on the commits page: 2026-09-11)
tradeoffs: Needs C++20 (buildable at C++17 with -DADM_CXX_STANDARD=17); GCC 14+ or Clang 19+ recommended, older compilers generate worse code. Compile time is long (compiled codelets up to radix 64 via xsimd and poet). Default -march=native binaries are not portable. Three interfaces: C++, C and an FFTW-subset drop-in (<admiral/fftw3.h>). Any size and rank, float/double/long double; no wisdom files (cost model at effort::estimate, plan-time race at automatic). Threads stay serial below about 32k elements.
caveats: Benchmark is run by the library author, and the same author wrote the fft_bench shootout repo (DiamonDinoia/fft_bench), so that repo is not independent evidence. The headline FFTW figure pools 19 1-D lengths and 9 N-D shapes and both precisions. In the fft_bench plots (images only, no numbers in the README) Admiral is roughly tied with MKL and FFTW over much of the 1-D range single-threaded on Xeon Platinum 8362, EPYC 7742 and EPYC 9474F, with MKL ahead at small sizes on Intel and FFTW ahead at small sizes on AMD, Sleef ahead at large sizes on EPYC 9474F, and multi-threaded MKL clearly ahead for large 1-D on the Intel node; that README also marks its MKL-omp numbers for rome and genoa as invalid. 16-thread 1-D vs threaded ducc0 is mixed per benchmark/README.md (geomean 0.33x to 1.82x by size). Very new project (earliest visible commit 2026-09-11), and the README says much of the code and cost-model tuning was done with Claude and that the author does not claim the fastest FFT. The licence is permissive with an attribution clause and may not be on the OSI list.

name: PhastFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.8 (via the Rust fftw 0.8.0 bindings); also RustFFT
workload: Single-threaded complex FFT of power-of-two lengths 8 to 8,388,608 in f32 and f64 (forward and inverse), median time per transform and heap memory allocated, using the divan benchmark crate on an M1 MacBook Pro.
claimed_speedup: Third-party run (astral4/fft-benchmark, phastft 0.2.1): f32 forward N=1024 4.749 us vs FFTW 7.291 us and RustFFT 7.707 us; N=65536 524.0 us vs 806.4 us vs 551.4 us; N=1,048,576 10.21 ms vs 14.20 ms vs 12.49 ms; N=8,388,608 109.0 ms vs 193.3 ms (RustFFT 103.9 ms is faster at 4M and 8M and at N=16 and 32). f64 N=1,048,576 15.10 ms vs FFTW 20.08 ms. Memory at N=1,048,576 f32: 8.388 MB vs RustFFT 41.94 MB. The project README also states 'up to 2x lower memory usage' vs RustFFT and shows plots against RustFFT and FFTW3 on an Apple M2.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (2024-05-03); FFTW built with Apple clang 15.0.0; cargo flags and FFTW configure options (NEON, planner flag) not stated
hardware: M1 MacBook Pro (third-party run); the project's own plots use a MacBook Air with Apple M2 (4P+4E, 24 GB, macOS 26.4.1)
tradeoffs: Rust crate with no C API, so use from C++ needs an FFI wrapper. Power-of-two sizes only (non-power-of-two unsupported, per the third-party report). In-place radix-2 with cache-oblivious recursion, CO-BRAVO SIMD bit reversal and optional multithreading; separate re/im array API is faster and lighter than the interleaved complex API, which allocates temporaries. The third-party report says phastft 0.2.1 needed nightly Rust for portable SIMD; the README now says SSE4.2, AVX2, NEON and WASM with runtime feature detection. RustFFT is faster for small sizes and handles arbitrary lengths.
caveats: The FFTW side of the third-party table looks unvectorised or planned cheaply: FFTW f32 needs 1.374 us at N=8 and 7.291 us at N=1024, far slower than FFTW NEON numbers reported elsewhere for M-series chips, and the FFTW build flags, planner mode (ESTIMATE vs MEASURE) and whether planning is inside the timed loop are not stated. The third-party repo is small and unreviewed, not a well-known suite (a verifier may reasonably demote B to C). It measured phastft 0.2.1 (2024); the crate is now at 0.4.1. The README's own comparison is plots only (no numbers). RustFFT beats PhastFT at the smallest and largest sizes, and for f64 at N=65536 and 2M to 8M.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): web search 'PhastFT RustFFT FFTW benchmark faster FFT library Rust' surfaced https://github.com/QuState/PhastFT and https://github.com/astral4/fft-benchmark

name: RustFFT
workload: Single-threaded complex FFT of power-of-two lengths 8 to 8,388,608 in f32 and f64, median time per transform, divan benchmark on an M1 MacBook Pro (third-party shootout of fftw, rustfft 6.2.0 and phastft 0.2.1).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (2024-05-03); FFTW built with Apple clang 15.0.0; cargo flags and FFTW configure options not stated
stars_or_usage: 942 stars; 30M+ crates.io downloads (30,150,241 at time of query)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C API (C++ use needs an FFI wrapper). Any length including primes in O(n log n); AVX and SSE4.1 on x86_64, NEON on AArch64, optional wasm SIMD. Planner chooses the algorithm; large non-power-of-two sizes are slower than power-of-two. Memory use is about 5x PhastFT's in the same shootout.
caveats: Evidence is a small third-party repo, not a well-known suite, and the FFTW side has unstated build flags and planner mode (FFTW absolute times look slow for an M1, and 1.374 us at N=8 suggests overhead inside the timed region). RustFFT's own README gives no FFTW numbers; a users.rust-lang.org post titled 'RustFFT 5.0.0-experimental.1 now faster than FFTW' exists but could not be opened from this environment. The third-party README conclusion that FFTW 'was consistently slower' than rustfft is contradicted by its own f32 table at N=1024 to 16384 forward. The only run found is on Apple silicon with rustfft 6.2.0; no x86 AVX comparison against FFTW was found.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): web search 'PhastFT RustFFT FFTW benchmark faster FFT library Rust' surfaced https://github.com/astral4/fft-benchmark; repo facts from https://github.com/ejmahler/RustFFT

name: AppleSiliconFFT
language: Metal Shading Language, Swift, C (SME2 kernels)
baseline: Apple vDSP (Accelerate) FFT; also Apple MPSGraph
workload: Batched 1-D complex FFT, N=4096 batch=256 (GFLOPS and microseconds per FFT) with Metal compute kernels on an Apple M1 GPU against CPU vDSP; the m6/ folder adds one-pass N=8192/16384 GPU kernels and a radix-8 FFT on the CPU's SME2 matrix unit measured on an Apple M6.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1, N=4096 batch=256: radix-8 Stockham 138.45 GFLOPS (1.78 us/FFT) vs vDSP 107.0 GFLOPS (2.29 us/FFT), +29%; in-place Cooley-Tukey with simdgroup_matrix 128 GFLOPS (+20%); radix-4 Stockham 113.6 GFLOPS (+6%). Apple M6: one-pass N=8192/16384 kernels 2.2x / 1.85x faster than MPSGraph (4.4x with FP16 storage); CPU SME2 radix-8 FFT beats vDSP by up to 5.3x.
compiler_and_flags: xcrun metal + metallib; swiftc -O -framework Metal -framework Accelerate; SME2 C kernels: clang -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 (toolchain versions not stated)
hardware: Apple M1 (main README, GPU kernels); Apple M6, macOS 27.0 (m6/README.md, SME2 and one-pass kernels)
tradeoffs: Apple Silicon only. GPU kernels are Metal shaders driven from Swift; the SME2 radix-8 FFT in m6/src/cpu/sme_fft.c/.h is plain C and callable from C++ but needs an M4 or later CPU. Fixed sizes per kernel (N=256 to 16384 multi-size set); no general planner. The 1-D GPU numbers are batch throughput.
caveats: GPU kernel against CPU vDSP, so the +29% is a batch-throughput comparison of different processors; how vDSP was threaded and batched is not stated in the README. The M1 headline is for one size (N=4096, batch 256); the multi-size table (N=256 to 16384) lists GFLOPS without vDSP columns. The M6 numbers are from a hardware generation and macOS 27.0 that a verifier may not be able to reproduce, and cold-cache runs differ from hot-cache by up to 3.7x per the m6 README. Results come from the author's own preprints (arXiv 2603.27569 and others), not peer reviewed as far as could be checked. Baseline is Apple-specific, not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): web search 'Beating vDSP Radix-8 Stockham FFT Apple Silicon github' (arXiv 2603.27569 listing) led to https://github.com/aminems/AppleSiliconFFT; m6 details from https://github.com/aminems/AppleSiliconFFT/blob/HEAD/m6/README.md

name: go-fft
baseline: FFTW 3.3.11 (native C, FFTW_MEASURE, threads=1); also numpy.fft, scipy.fft (pocketfft) and gonum/dsp/fourier
workload: Steady-state (plan reused) complex 1-D, real 1-D and complex 2-D FFTs in float64 on an Apple M4 Max, ns/op and GFLOP/s, with go-fft's 2-D path using several goroutines and every reference single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: Not faster than FFTW in 1-D: lags 1.17x to 3.28x on complex 1-D rows (e.g. N=1,024 3,395 ns vs FFTW 2,127 ns). Faster only on the 2-D multicore rows: 256x256 208,437 ns vs 271,098 ns; 512x512 633,920 ns vs 1,247,215 ns; 1024x1024 2,784,623 ns vs 6,301,688 ns. Vs scipy.fft (pocketfft) complex 1-D: N=256 716 ns vs 2,302 ns; N=1,024 3,395 ns vs 4,470 ns; N=65,536 377,784 ns vs 499,500 ns (slower at N=1,048,576: 13.36 ms vs 8.04 ms). Report summary: at or above parity with FFTW on 3 of 24 ops and with gonum on 19 of 19; 'typically 3-5x on composite N' faster than gonum.
compiler_and_flags: go1.26.4 darwin/arm64 (CGO=0 pure Go); FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew arm64 bottle with NEON, plans FFTW_MEASURE threads=1; numpy 2.5.0 and scipy 1.18.0 pinned single-threaded
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, so not callable from C++ without a wrapper. Arbitrary lengths: mixed radix for 13-smooth lengths, Rader for primes whose N-1 is 7-smooth, large-prime convolution otherwise (BENCHMARKS.md shows FFTW ahead at primes 1,009 and 10,007 by 1.26x and 2.15x). AVX2 and NEON SIMD butterflies. Plan creation is far cheaper than FFTW_MEASURE (e.g. 14,808 ns vs 3,434,000 ns at N=1,024).
caveats: Does not beat FFTW on the single-threaded rows; the only wins are 2-D shapes where go-fft fans rows and columns across goroutines while FFTW, numpy and scipy are single-threaded, so the 2-D comparison is not apples-to-apples. The report states real 1-D transforms lag FFTW by 1.51x to 3.20x. Recent commits are co-authored by an AI assistant and the repo is a few months old (earliest visible commit 2026-06-20). The README attributes part of the scipy gap at small N to Python FFI overhead on the scipy side, so the scipy comparison there is not like-for-like. Listed mainly because it is a benchmark-backed pure-Go FFT that beats the Go incumbent gonum and, at some sizes, scipy.fft.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): web search 'github FFT library faster than FFTW README benchmark AVX2 AVX-512 NEON header-only' surfaced https://github.com/go-fft/fft/pull/12; numbers from BENCHMARKS.md

name: minfft
workload: One-dimensional double-precision in-place forward complex DFT of size N=2 to 2^20, speed in MFLOPS, plotted against KissFFT, PocketFFT and a machine-specific SSE2 FFTW (docs/speed.svg).
claimed_speedup: README says its speed and accuracy are compared with 'libraries of similar design - KissFFT and PocketFFT', with FFTW shown for reference; the plot has no numbers in text. Digitised from the data points of docs/speed.svg (derived from page data, approximate, axes log2(N) and MFLOPS): minfft is above KissFFT at every size, about 1.4x to 4.8x, median about 2.0x (e.g. N=2^10 about 8,200 vs 5,000 MFLOPS); about on par with PocketFFT (median about 0.9x, lower for N>=2^10) and about 0.55x of FFTW SSE2.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two lengths only, any dimensionality; complex and real DFT and DCT/DST types 2 to 4. Double precision by default (single via MINFFT_SINGLE). C89 and Fortran 2003 interfaces, in-place or out-of-place, auxiliary data object per plan. Split-radix (2/4) DIF algorithm, 'simple means' rather than hand-tuned SIMD; far slower than FFTW with SIMD.
caveats: First-party plot with no stated CPU, compiler or flags, and the ratios above were read from SVG coordinates, not from quoted numbers. It is not faster than PocketFFT at large sizes. The README plots are the only performance evidence found; a separate repo, NotoriousLOB/Notorious-FFT, reports its own header-only FFT beating minfft by 1.08x to 1.13x on an ARM Cortex-A78AE, which suggests minfft is a reasonable small-library reference but is not evidence for minfft's speed.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): benchFFT benchees list (https://github.com/FFTW/benchfft/tree/master/benchees) includes minfft; README performance section of https://github.com/aimukhin/minfft and docs/speed.svg

name: OTFFT
baseline: FFTW 3 (and Ooura's FFT, per the bundled benchmark)
workload: The upstream package ships fftbench1 (excludes FFT object initialisation) and fftbench2 (includes it) that time OTFFT against FFTW3 and Ooura's FFT; no results are published in any page that could be opened here.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on any opened page. The upstream OTFFT homepage (wwwa.pikara.ne.jp/okojisan/otfft-en/) is titled 'OTFFT -- FFT library using AVX that is faster than FFTW' according to a search snippet, but that page is blocked in this environment and was not opened.
stars_or_usage: 29 stars (DEWETRON fork); 13 stars (akinomyoga/OTFFT 6.5 fork); included in the kfrlib/fft-benchmark suite
tradeoffs: C++ template-metaprogramming Stockham FFT with AVX/AVX-512 and six-step algorithm, mixed radix; heavy compile time; the original expects an auto-tuning step (ffttune) and a source build for the target CPU. The DEWETRON fork adds multi-ISA builds (AVX2, AVX, SSE2), unit tests and standard OpenMP and keeps pace with upstream 11.5. Complex-to-complex, real-to-complex, Bluestein and DCT supported.
caveats: No numeric evidence was opened, so this is tier D by default and a verifier with access to the original homepage or the kfrlib/fft-benchmark results should re-tier it. The DEWETRON repo is a maintained fork of upstream source by OK Ojisan (Takuya Okahisa), upstream homepage not a git repo; the other fork akinomyoga/OTFFT is based on the older OTFFT-6.5. Both GitHub repos last committed in 2021-2022.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): web search 'github FFT library faster than FFTW README benchmark' surfaced the OTFFT homepage title; https://github.com/kfrlib/fft-benchmark lists OTFFT among benchmarked libraries; README of https://github.com/akinomyoga/OTFFT mentions the bundled FFTW3 and Ooura benchmark

name: PFFFT (per-CPU benchmark results by hayguen/pffft_benchmarks)
workload: Single-precision 1-D complex and real FFTs of power-of-two sizes 16 to 1,048,576 with SIMD, in MFLOPS (5*N*log2(N) for complex, 2.5*N*log2(N) for real), on an Intel Xeon Gold 6130 with gcc 8.3.0; the repo holds 20+ per-CPU result files (ARM Cortex-A9/A15, Raspberry Pi 3B+/4B, Atom N270, Core 2, i5/i7 generations, Apple A8X).
claimed_speedup: Xeon Gold 6130, complex single precision: PFFFT (ordered) vs KissFFT at N=1,024 21,283 vs 5,184 MFLOPS (4.1x, relative duration column 4.106) and at N=1,048,576 11,230 vs 2,390 (4.7x); real N=1,024 24,027 vs 4,247 (5.7x). Vs FFTW: FFTW(auto) is faster on complex (N=1,024 49,696 MFLOPS vs PFFFT 21,283), PFFFT wins only at N>=524,288 against FFTW(estim) (N=1,048,576 11,230 vs 5,719 MFLOPS, 1.96x derived from page data); on real data PFFFT is about even to 8% faster than FFTW(auto) at N=512 to 2,048 (relative duration of FFTW(auto) 1.014, 1.078, 1.005) and the unordered PFFFT-U has a 10-17% shorter duration than ordered PFFFT at N=64 to 2,048 (relative duration 0.83 to 0.92).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3.0 per the file name; optimisation flags not stated in the results file (the benchmark CMake uses -DBENCH_ARCH=native per hayguen/pffft README)
tradeoffs: Licence is described as BSD-like with no SPDX id in the READMEs (LICENSE.txt in hayguen/pffft). Single-precision 1-D only in the original; sizes must be multiples of 16 (complex) or 32 (real) with SIMD; the benchmarks use the ordered transform for PFFFT and report the faster unordered variant separately.
caveats: Evidence for an already-catalogued project (marton78/pffft). The results are tables and plots from the pffft fork maintainer, not a neutral third party, and the results file does not state compiler flags. FFTW(auto) is recorded as 0.000000 for N>=4096 (not measured), so the FFTW comparison above 2,048 rests on FFTW(estim). FFTW is clearly faster than PFFFT on complex data up to about 262,144 points, which fits the README's own statement that PFFFT aims to be at least 50% as fast as the fastest FFT.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): https://github.com/hayguen/pffft_benchmarks (found via web search 'hayguen pffft_benchmarks results'); file list from https://github.com/hayguen/pffft_benchmarks/tree/master

name: dft_simd
baseline: FFTW 3 (single-precision plans through the FFTW API, including its bulk/advanced interface)
workload: Bulk transformation of 2^24 (16.8 million) short single-precision real-to-complex DFTs, 60 samples in the original test and 1024 samples in the 2025 update, with codelets generated by FFTW's genfft and compiled for AVX/AVX2/AVX512 vector types so that 8 (or 16) transforms run side by side ('vertical' SIMD).
claimed_speedup: 2025, AMD EPYC 9474F single core: 60-sample AVX2 codelet with fixed strides 79 ms vs FFTW aligned single-DFT plan 858 ms (10.8x per the README); 1024-sample AVX2 7,270 ms vs 12,136 ms (1.67x, derived from page data) and AVX512 10,610 ms vs 24,657 ms (2.3x). 2018, MacBook Pro i5-5287U: 8-transform 60-sample codelet 379 ms vs best FFTW plan 1,912 ms (about 5x) and 207 ms with compile-time strides.
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo; Apple LLVM 9.0.0 (clang-900.0.39.2) for the 2018 MacBook run and gcc 4.8.5 for the Xeon E5-2650 v4 run; compiler for the 2025 EPYC run not stated; FFTW from MacPorts for the 2018 run
hardware: AMD EPYC 9474F single core (2025 table); Intel Core i5-5287U MacBook Pro (2018 text); also Xeon E5-2650 v4
tradeoffs: A technique and test harness, not a general FFT library: only fixed-size codelets are in the repo (60-sample and 1024-sample real-to-complex), generated with FFTW's OCaml genfft and compiled per size and ISA, and compile time grows sharply with size. Input must be laid out as arrays of SIMD vectors (8 floats for AVX, 16 for AVX512), so it only helps when many short transforms are available at once; runtime strides cost about 2x unless fixed at compile time.
caveats: First-party benchmark of a bulk short-DFT workload where FFTW's horizontal SIMD is known to be inefficient, so it does not show a win on single large transforms. The README does not say whether packing and unpacking into SIMD layout is inside the timed region. The 2025 EPYC table has no stated compiler or FFTW build flags (tier A rests on the 2018 runs, which do name compiler, build type and CPU). GPLv2 inherited from FFTW codelet generators; the author notes the copyright status of machine-generated code is unclear.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): https://github.com/topics/fourier-transform?l=c%2B%2B listing flagged sfegan/dft_simd; numbers from its README
